title: Who is Behind the Avatar?  Verifying Teleoperator Identity in Reenacted Avatar Videos

pages.title: Overview
pages.content: Welcome to the first International Competition on **Teleoperator Identity Verification in Reenacted Avatar Videos — WBA 2026**. ## Motivation Photorealistic avatars are increasingly used in telepresence, mixed reality, gaming, virtual environments, and AI-mediated video communication. In these settings, the visible face may be synthetic or may differ entirely from the person controlling it. Consequently, conventional face-recognition methods may not be sufficient to verify the identity of the underlying user. The **Who Is Behind the Avatar? (WBA)** challenge investigates whether behavioral information preserved in avatar videos can be used to authenticate the human teleoperator independently of the avatar’s visual appearance. Unlike conventional DeepFake-detection challenges, WBA does not ask participants to determine whether a video is real or synthetic. Avatar-generated videos are treated as legitimate communication media. The objective is instead to verify **operator authenticity**: whether an avatar is controlled by the authorized person. ## Challenge Task WBA 2026 is a **cross-avatar teleoperator verification challenge**. For each verification trial, participants are provided with: 1. a gallery avatar video driven by a known teleoperator; and 2. a probe avatar video driven by an unknown teleoperator. Participants must determine whether the two avatar videos are driven by: * the **same teleoperator**, representing a genuine trial; or * **different teleoperators**, representing an impostor trial. The gallery and probe videos may represent the same person through different avatar identities. Therefore, systems should focus on teleoperator-specific behavioral information rather than the visible appearance of the avatar. Potential behavioral cues include: * facial-motion dynamics * head movement and pose * expression timing * gaze behavior * speech-related facial movement * temporal motion patterns * other person-specific behavioral characteristics Participants may develop systems using RGB video, facial landmarks, head-pose features, expression dynamics, temporal motion descriptors, video embeddings, or other suitable representations. ## Dataset The source driving videos were collected in Japan during controlled dyadic online first-meeting conversations. The selected sequences are taken from the self-introduction portion of the conversations and include both speaking and listening segments. The original recordings were captured under controlled frontal-camera and lighting conditions. However, the original human videos are retained by the organizers and are not released to challenge participants. Instead, the motion and expression information from the original recordings are transferred to photorealistic avatar templates through a face-reenactment pipeline. The avatar appearances are selected from the publicly available **NVFAIR** dataset, while the reenacted videos are generated using **GAGAvatar**. This design reduces the direct exposure of the original participants’ visual identities while preserving motion and behavioral information relevant to teleoperator verification. Audio is not included in the released dataset and is not used during evaluation.

pages.title: Participation
pages.content: The competition is open to everyone. Important: Please register using your institutional email. Registrations with gmail.com or qq.com email addresses will not be approved. As well, the Team Leader must sign the license aggreement. If you are student, your supervisor must sign. Data sharing Policy: When releasing the data for the competition, participants will be required to agree to use it for "Academic use only". The dataset will be provided exclusively to registered participating teams and is strictly limited to use for the challenge. If you have any questions or need further assistance, please don’t hesitate to reach out to ammar@yy.d3c.osaka-u.ac.jp and cc: allam@yy.d3c.osaka-u.ac.jp We will provide You can use the following repo to extract the data, [Starter kit](https://github.com/jasam-sheja/OUMVLP-OF-challenge). ## Released Resources The organizers plan to provide: * training data * test-data access instructions * official verification trial lists * a baseline embedding and similarity system * evaluation code * a sample submission * a submission-validation tool * competition rules and documentation The baseline system is intended to support reproducibility, reduce the entry barrier, and encourage participants to investigate stronger temporal and behavioral representations. ## Data-Use Policy The challenge data may only be used in accordance with the official WBA 2026 participation rules and the licenses associated with the source datasets and avatar-generation resources. Participants must not attempt to recover, identify, manually label, or disclose the identities of individuals represented in the hidden evaluation data. Access to hidden labels, avatar-template identities, or unauthorized annotations is prohibited. Any external datasets, pretrained models, or additional resources used by participants must be disclosed in the team’s technical report and must comply with their applicable licenses.

pages.title: Evaluation
pages.content:
## Training and Test Protocol

The training and test sets are disjoint with respect to both:

* teleoperator identity; and
* avatar appearance.

No teleoperator appearing in the test set is included in the training set. Similarly, the avatar templates used for testing are not included in the training data.

This protocol evaluates whether submitted systems can generalize to:

* unseen teleoperators;
* unseen avatar identities;
* different speaking conditions;
* variations in avatar geometry and motion response.

The challenge is designed to discourage reliance on avatar appearance and encourage the development of representations that capture persistent teleoperator-specific behavioral characteristics.

## Submission

Participants are required to generate and submit an embedding for every test video.

For each verification pair, the submitted gallery and probe embeddings are compared using one of the following measures:

* cosine similarity or cosine distance; or
* Euclidean distance.

Participants specify the comparison method used by their system at submission time.

The Codabench evaluation program calculates the verification scores and corresponding performance metrics from the submitted embeddings.

## Evaluation

The official evaluation metrics are:

* **Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve — AUC**
* **Equal Error Rate — EER**

Teams are ranked exclusively according to **AUC**.

EER is reported as an additional reference metric and is not used to determine the final leaderboard ranking.

Performance is evaluated under three conditions:

### Speaking Condition

Both the gallery and probe videos contain speaking sequences.

### Non-Speaking Condition

Both the gallery and probe videos contain listening or non-speaking sequences.

### Cross-Condition

One video contains a speaking sequence, while the other contains a non-speaking sequence.

The final leaderboard score is calculated as the **average AUC across the three evaluation conditions**.

pages.title: Prizes
pages.content:
We are excited to recognize the outstanding achievements of **the top three teams**  in this competition with the following rewards:

1. **Award Certificates**: All members of the winning teams will receive official certificates of achievement.
2. **ACCV workshop submission Co-Authorship**: Up to three members per team (from the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd-place teams) will be invited as co-authors on a competition-related paper to be submitted to 18th Asian Conference on Computer Vision (ACCV)

This is a unique opportunity to gain academic recognition, contribute to cutting-edge research, and enhance your professional profile.
